title: Indexes in PostgreSQL
idea: An index is a separate sorted structure on a column. It lets Postgres find matching rows without reading the whole table.
points: Without an index, Postgres does a sequential scan: it reads every row.
The default index type is a B-tree: sorted keys that point at table rows.
`create index` builds one; `primary key` and `unique` constraints build theirs for you.
Each index uses disk space and slows writes: index columns you search by.

steps.caption: No index: Postgres reads rows in table order. It reaches Dune at row 5.
It still reads to the end: another Dune could follow, so it checks every row.
With an index on `title`, the lookup starts at the root. Dune sorts before Gilead, so it takes the first leaf.
The leaf page holds the key Dune and a pointer to its table row.
One more jump reaches the row: three page reads here instead of sixteen row reads.
Real pages hold many more keys, so the tree stays only a few levels deep.

code.title: Ask Postgres for its plan
code.caption: A lookup by title on 20,003 books, planned three ways. It prints plan types, not timings, which change on every run.

walk.text: `explain (format json)` returns the plan as data. We keep its node type and index name.
The Book Store table with its three seed books.
20,000 filler rows give the index work to save. Their titles look like `Book 1`.
`analyze` refreshes the statistics the planner reads. Postgres also does this itself, in the background.
With no index on `title`, Postgres must read the whole table.
Build the index, refresh the statistics, ask again. The planner now chooses differently.
The index holds `title`, not `lower(title)`, so this query cannot use it.

code.title: The index in a Drizzle schema
code.caption: The third argument of `pgTable` lists indexes. `npx drizzle-kit generate` writes the migration and `npx drizzle-kit migrate` applies it.

pitfalls: A function on the column, such as `lower(title)`, stops a plain index being used.
Postgres often scans a tiny table anyway: test indexes with realistic row counts.
A leading wildcard, as in `like '%une'`, cannot use a B-tree index.

quiz.why: The index is sorted by `title`, not `lower(title)`, so the first query scans every row. The second matches the index.

takeaway: Index the columns you search by; check the plan with `explain`.
